```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

The classical joinpoint model is a least squares fit to a rate, with
joinpoints at the observed years. Three common situations stretch it: the
data are counts and their likelihood is known, the series has a seasonal
pattern that is not part of the trend, and the trend changes between two
observations. This vignette shows the extensions that handle each.

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Counts: Poisson and binomial joinpoint models

When the data are counts of events, a generalized linear model uses their
distribution directly: a Poisson regression with the population as
exposure for rates, or a logistic regression for proportions (Czajkowski
et al. 2008). The model is fitted by maximum likelihood for every admissible
placement of the joinpoints, and the placement with the smallest deviance
is the estimate.

Births with obesity class III in Ontario are binomial counts out of all
births of the year. A logistic joinpoint model, fitted by maximum
likelihood, and the least squares model of the log prevalence:

```{r}
ob <- subset(ontario_bmi, category == "Obesity class III")
fit_bin <- joinpoint(ob, year, count = count, population = births,
                     family = "binomial", type = "percent", kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic")
fit_ls <- joinpoint(ob, year, count = count, population = births,
                    type = "percent", kmax = 2, method = "bic",
                    ci_method = "parametric")
knitr::kable(jp_table(fit_bin))
knitr::kable(jp_table(fit_ls))
```

Both fits place the joinpoint in 2015, and for a rare outcome the change in
the odds is practically the change in the prevalence, so the estimates
agree. The intervals do not. A maximum likelihood fit fixes the dispersion
at 1: it assumes that the yearly proportions vary only as binomial sampling
of about 115,000 births allows. The model selection table shows that they
vary more:

```{r}
crit <- model_selection(fit_bin)$criteria
crit[, c("joinpoints", "deviance", "df", "dispersion", "bic", "selected")]
```

The selected model leaves a deviance of `r round(crit$deviance[crit$selected], 1)`
on `r crit$df[crit$selected]` degrees of freedom, several times what binomial
variation would produce. With `overdispersion = TRUE` the dispersion is
estimated from the Pearson statistic of the largest model (quasi-likelihood),
and every Wald standard error on the log odds scale grows by its square
root:

```{r}
fit_qb <- joinpoint(ob, year, count = count, population = births,
                    family = "binomial", type = "percent", kmax = 2,
                    method = "bic", overdispersion = TRUE)
model_selection(fit_qb)$criteria$dispersion[1]
knitr::kable(jp_table(fit_qb))
```

The remaining difference from least squares has another source. Wald
intervals come from the joint fit of all segments with normal quantiles,
whereas the least squares intervals come from separate regressions of each
segment with t quantiles on few degrees of freedom. Both condition on the
estimated joinpoint; the interval of the joinpoint itself comes from the
profile deviance.

The number of joinpoints of a likelihood model can also be chosen by a
sequential Monte Carlo likelihood ratio test, which simulates counts from
the fitted null model (`method = "lrt"`, with the dispersion fixed at 1).
The joinpoints of every model, observed or simulated, are found by fitting
all admissible placements, so they are the maximum likelihood joinpoints.

## Seasons: covariates

Monthly series often follow a seasonal cycle that would otherwise be
mistaken for joinpoints or inflate the residual variance. Covariates enter
every segment with common coefficients and are centered, so the trend is
reported at their average. The data below are simulated: monthly visits
that rise by 1% a month, then fall by 2% a month after month 40, with a
seasonal swing.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
visits <- data.frame(month = 1:72, calendar = rep(1:12, 6))
visits$rate <- exp(3 + 0.01 * visits$month -
                     0.03 * pmax(visits$month - 40, 0) +
                     0.3 * sin(2 * pi * visits$calendar / 12) +
                     rnorm(72, sd = 0.02))
fit_season <- joinpoint(visits, month, rate, kmax = 2,
                        covariates = ~ factor(calendar),
                        interval = "Monthly", ci_method = "parametric")
fit_season
```

The monthly percent changes of 1.0% and -2.0% and the joinpoint at month
40 are recovered. The plot shows the observed values, seasonal swing
included, and the trend at the average season:

```{r}
autoplot(fit_season) + labs(x = "Month", y = "Visits per 1,000")
```

## Joinpoints between observations

The grid search places joinpoints at observed values, or at a few points in
between (`jp_control(n_grid = )`). The trend may well have changed between
two observations. Hudson (1966) showed how to find the exact least squares
location: inside a gap between two observations the model is linear in a
hinge and a step at the next observation, and the joinpoint follows from
their coefficients. With `continuous = TRUE` every placement of the
joinpoints, at observations or inside gaps, is examined, so the solution is
the least squares fit. A joinpoint may also sit exactly on an observation
that the placement rules require on one side: the limit of placements just
beside it, which counts the observation toward one of its two segments.

The published analysis of the Ontario mean BMI placed one joinpoint at
fiscal year 2016. Freed from the grid, the one joinpoint model moves:

```{r}
mb <- unique(ontario_bmi[c("year", "births", "mean_bmi", "sd_bmi")])
mb$se <- mb$sd_bmi / sqrt(mb$births)
fit_cont <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmin = 1,
                      kmax = 1, continuous = TRUE)
fit_grid <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmin = 1,
                      kmax = 1, ci_method = "parametric")
fit_cont
sse <- c(continuous = fit_cont$fits[[1]]$models[["1"]]$sse,
         grid = fit_grid$fits[[1]]$models[["1"]]$sse)
sse
joinpoints(fit_cont)[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]
```

The continuous estimate, `r round(joinpoints(fit_cont)$estimate, 3)`, falls
between fiscal years 2015 and 2016 and fits better than the grid solution
(residual sum of squares `r sprintf("%.1f", sse[1])` against
`r sprintf("%.1f", sse[2])`), with a flat first segment. The interval of the
joinpoint, whose limits are located inside the gaps where the profile sum of
squares crosses the cutoff, runs from
`r sprintf("%.1f", joinpoints(fit_cont)$lower)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", joinpoints(fit_cont)$upper)`: the data cannot pin the
turn to a single year.

```{r}
autoplot(fit_cont, error_bars = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = expression("Mean BMI (kg/m"^2 * ")"))
```

Freedom has a price. Allowing two joinpoints, the continuous search
isolates the jump between 2016 and 2017 as a segment of its own, with both
of its observations on its joinpoints, and BIC prefers it:

```{r}
fit_two <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", continuous = TRUE)
apc(fit_two)[, c("start", "end", "estimate")]
```

Such a segment describes two yearly values, not a trend. Requiring three
observations between joinpoints rules it out and restores the one
joinpoint model:

```{r}
fit_three <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmax = 2,
                       method = "bic", continuous = TRUE,
                       control = jp_control(min_obs_between = 3))
fit_three$fits[[1]]$k_selected
```

Continuous joinpoints are fitted with parametric intervals and selection by
a criterion; the empirical quantile method and the permutation test would
need the same search for every resampled data set.

## References

Czajkowski M, Gill R, Rempala G (2008). Model selection in logistic
joinpoint regression with applications to analyzing cohort mortality
patterns. *Statistics in Medicine* 27:1508-1526.

Hudson DJ (1966). Fitting segmented curves whose join points have to be
estimated. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 61:1097-1129.
